another.title: Mental multiplication: 43 times 6
paragraphs: Think of it like pushing a cart through a grocery store while adding up your bill in your head. You pick up a bag of rice at 6 dollars, then a jar of sauce at 4, and you say to yourself, ten so far. That running total is the thing you are holding on to. Then you pick up cheese at 5, and now you have to do something with the number you are holding: add 5 to it and replace it with 15.

Notice that two jobs are going on at once. One job is keeping the total alive between aisles, and the other is working on it every time a new price shows up. If all you did was keep it, you would just be staring at a number. If all you did was add, you would have nothing to add to. And the two jobs share one small amount of mental room. That is why a friend calling out a question halfway down the aisle makes the total vanish. Your limited capacity got used for something else, and the held number slipped away.

So when you explain the 43 times 6 problem to a friend, you can say it works the same way. The 8 is like the running total you keep carrying, and the multiplying and adding are like the new prices you keep folding in. Working memory is not a shelf where numbers sit. It is the shared workspace where you keep something and work on it at the very same time, and losing the kept piece ruins the answer.

another.title: Tower of Hanoi with subgoals
paragraphs: Imagine you are moving a heavy piano into the back bedroom. The piano is in the living room, but a couple of chairs are stacked on top of it, and the back bedroom is full of boxes. You cannot just go straight at the goal, because the piano will not budge while it is buried and the room it is headed for is not clear.

So you stop asking how to move the piano and start asking what is stopping you. First, the chairs have to come off, so you set them to the side in the hallway. Second, the bedroom has to be emptied, so the boxes get shoved temporarily into the hall too. Only then does the piano roll in, and that is the real prize. Along the way you did things that looked pointless, like lifting chairs just to put them down somewhere else, but each one removed a specific obstacle. And when the piano is in place, you are not done, because the chairs and boxes still have to be arranged around it.

That is how you can tell a friend what subgoals do in the Tower of Hanoi. You look at the gap between where you are and where you want to be, you spot what blocks the biggest move, and you make clearing that block its own small goal. Parking a small disk somewhere temporarily is just like setting the chairs in the hall. Getting the big disk into place is the piano landing in the bedroom, and the rest of the work still follows.

another.title: Mutilated checkerboard
paragraphs: Picture a school dance with 62 students in the gym, and the teacher says every single student must dance in a pair made of one leader and one follower. It sounds fine at first, because 62 people can form 31 pairs. Without looking any closer, you might start matching up students and shuffling them around, trying pair after pair, and you could be at it all evening.

Now suppose someone looks at the name tags and sees that 32 students are wearing leader tags and only 30 are wearing follower tags. The question is settled in a second. Each pair needs exactly one of each kind, so thirty-one pairs would call for thirty-one of each, and the room simply does not have that. No amount of shuffling could fix it, because the problem was never about the total head count. It was about the two kinds.

This is the same move that makes the checkerboard click. The two removed corners are the same color, which is like sending home two followers and leaving the leaders short of partners. A domino is a pair that always needs one dark square and one light square, so once you label the squares by color and count, the answer appears before you place a single domino. You can tell your friend that the numbers matching up is not enough. What matters is whether the kinds match up, and the way you describe the squares is what lets you see that.

another.title: Chain problem
paragraphs: Say you are making one big closed bracelet loop out of four short strands of beads, and each strand ends in a little metal ring. A jeweler will open and close rings for you, but your budget only covers opening and closing three rings. The first idea that comes to mind is to open a ring on the end of every strand and hook each one to the next strand. That is four rings, and you can only afford three, so the plan fails when you count it up.

The way out is to stop treating every strand the same. Most strands are things to be joined, but one strand can be sacrificed as a supply of parts. You take the three rings of a single strand, open each one once, and use them as connectors to link the other three strands into the loop. The strand you gave up stops being a strand with beads in the way you expected and becomes a bag of connectors, and the count now comes to exactly three.

That is the whole trick behind the chain problem, and it is a good way to explain it aloud. Your first idea was to open one link on every piece, which costs too much. The better idea is to open all the links of a single piece and let it serve as the connectors for the others. Nothing about it comes from trying the first plan slightly harder. You have to change what you think of one piece as, and that sudden change in how you see the parts is what insight feels like.

another.title: Triangle problem
paragraphs: Imagine a coach arranges a team photo with players standing in rows of one, two, three and four, ten players in all, narrow at the front and wide at the back, so the formation points forward. Now the coach says to flip it so it points the other way, but only three players are allowed to move and the other seven must stay put. The natural instinct is to nudge everybody a little, one step this way, one step that way, hoping it slowly turns into the new shape. It never gets there, because small nudges keep the old shape intact.

What works is to stop looking at it as a fixed shape and start seeing it as a set of people who can be regrouped. Most of the team can stay where they are, because they already form part of a row that will still be needed. The few who move are the ones who were forming the old point and the old base. They go to the opposite end, and the row that was tiny becomes the wide one, while the wide one becomes tiny.

This is the same shift as in the triangle problem, and you can tell a friend that is why it feels sudden. Until you let go of the picture of the formation pointing one way, you do not feel any closer, even though you are working hard. Then the regrouping appears all at once, and you jump from feeling cold to knowing you have it. That jump, rather than steady progress, is the signature of insight.

another.title: Water-jug problems and mental set
paragraphs: Think about walking to class. For weeks you have taken the main road, and it has never failed you. You stop even thinking about it, and your feet just take you there. Then one morning a new footpath opens through the park, and it would get you there in half the time. But you are on autopilot, and you walk right past the entrance without noticing it.

What is interesting is that the main road did not stop working. It still gets you to class every time. The trouble is that because it worked so many times, you stopped looking around for anything else. Your past success made one way feel like the only way, so the shorter way was sitting in plain view and you missed it. Someone new to campus, with no habit, would probably spot the footpath at once.

That is what a mental set is, and it is how you can explain the water-jug problems to a friend. The early problems all got solved by the same longer recipe, so people kept running it by habit. When later problems arrived where a quick one-step answer was available, the old recipe still worked, but it kept them from noticing the easier route. A habit that serves you well when problems look alike can quietly get in the way once the problems change.
